schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch summarise the whole scene of mourning to the king's gate; Ellicott notes the grief is described in outward signs alone, with no prayer to the God of Israel, unlike Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah who besought him.
Clarke adds the Greek cry that a guiltless people are to be destroyed; Wesley reads the loud cry as Mordecai's sense of the coming mischief, bravely espousing a just cause.
Gill weighs how Mordecai learned of the decree (report, common fame, or the posted edict), and reports the Targums' supernatural revelation by Elijah or the Holy Ghost.
Henry reads the public grief as a noble, conscientious espousal of a righteous and sinking cause, Mordecai committing himself to him that judgeth righteously.

Keil fixes 'before the king's gate' as the open space none might enter in mourning; Ellicott finds the rule meant nothing sad or ill-omened should meet the monarch's gaze, as if to evade sorrow, sickness, and death.
Clarke: the mourner's habit barred Mordecai from the gate by law; Wesley: the sackcloth was shut out lest it grieve the king, but what avails barring the tokens of sorrow while its causes press in?
Henry satirises a court that forbids sackcloth but cannot forbid sickness and death (cf. soft clothing in kings' palaces, Matt. 11:8), so Mordecai must keep before the gate.
Gill: Mordecai pressed as near the gate as he might, that Esther might be made acquainted with the calamity.

Keil renders 'sackcloth and ashes spread for many' as sitting in hairy garments on strewn ashes (cf. Isa. 58:5); Ellicott notes the provincial grief too is set down in outward signs only, with no word of entreaty.
Henry: the Jews denied themselves table and bed, and those who stayed in captivity against God's call now perhaps repented their folly too late.
Clarke marvels that in all the fasting, weeping, and wailing there is not the slightest intimation of praying to God.
Gill traces the mourning to every province the destroying decree reached.

Keil renders Esther's reaction as convulsive grief and reads the raiment as sent to enable Mordecai to enter and give particulars; Ellicott infers her tie to Mordecai was known to her household, not yet to the king.
Clarke: she supposed Mordecai had been stripped of clothing; Wesley: she clothed him that he might return to his place or come to tell her the cause of his grief.

Henry: the queen forgot not her relation, grieving for the affliction of Joseph though anointed with chief ointments (Amos 6:6); Mordecai refused the robe, as one refusing comfort, to make her feel his grief.
Gill: the maids told it as startling news, and inferred a peculiar respect between Esther and Mordecai.

themes: grief that will not be comforted

schools.summary: Keil describes the errand: Esther sends Hatach to learn what Mordecai's mourning meant and why.
Clarke: the eunuch was set to serve her and to observe her, for no despot escapes jealousy and suspicion.
Henry: the harem's strict confinement forced all commerce through a trusted messenger; to enquire after the church's trouble, that we may direct our griefs and prayers, becomes all that love Zion.
Gill names Hatach the trusted chamberlain and rejects the Targum's identification of him with Daniel as chronologically impossible.

outliers.note: Notes the Targum's identification of Hatach with Daniel, which he rejects, since Daniel could not have lived to this time.

themes: a servant who is also a watcher

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'street' as the broad open place, the Hebrew rehob; Keil sets the meeting in the open space before the king's gate, where Mordecai laid the matter out.
Henry: the king's wives were so confined that no direct conference was possible, and every word had to pass by Hatach's hand.
Gill has Hatach go out to Mordecai in the street, where he stood publicly showing his grief.

themes: the open square before the gate
the mourner barred, the queen walled in

schools.summary: Keil fixes on the exact sum Haman promised to weigh into the king's treasuries, brought forward as the chief point of the report — the price of a people's life.

Henry reads the message as an authentic account with a charge to intercede, and relays the Jewish legend of the three schoolchildren whose lessons (Prov. 3:25; Isa. 8:10; Isa. 46:4) comforted Mordecai.
Gill: Mordecai told how his refusal to reverence Haman drew ruin on himself and all the Jews, and Haman's vowed revenge and scheme.

themes: the price of the Jews' destruction

schools.summary: Keil describes the double commission: the copy of the Susa decree to show her, and the charge to command her to go in and make supplication for her people.
Clarke notes the Greek text's tender addition to the charge ('remember thy low estate... pray to the Lord'), absent from the Hebrew, Syriac, and Vulgate.
Henry: the true copy was sent that she might see the danger and rectify the misinformations imposed on the king, not doubting he would vacate the decree.
Gill: the edict being published in the city, Mordecai had seen and transcribed it.

themes: the Greek addition to the charge

schools.summary: Keil carries the narrative on: hearing the report, Esther at once sent word back to Mordecai by the same hand.
Henry keeps before us the machinery of the conference — every message borne faithfully by the trusted eunuch between gate and palace.
Gill: Hatach told Esther the words of Mordecai — the case of the Jews, its cause, and what he would have her do.

themes: the burden crosses into the palace
a summons touching her own life

schools.summary: Ellicott notes 'Again' has nothing in the original and should read 'and,' the reply running on continuously from v.9; Keil marks the fresh commission introducing her account of the law.
Gill: she must speak again through Hatach, the wives of kings being wholly under such attendants' watch.

themes: the reply sent by the eunuch

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'one law' for the unbidden, notes the Persepolis kings always grasping the sceptre, and contrasts the deadly Persian throne with the King of kings who bids men come to his footstool.

Clarke expounds the divine majesty affected by Persian kings and suspects Haman kept Esther from the king thirty days to alienate him; Wesley reads the law as guarding the king's majesty and safety and hears Esther's fear of cooling affection.
Henry judges the law made in pride not prudence, a foolish rule making the palace a prison — unlike the throne of grace we may come to boldly through the blood of Jesus.
Gill stresses how notorious the law was, known even to the meanest subject.

themes: the law of the golden sceptre
the throne of grace by contrast

schools.summary: Keil marks the turn: when Esther's words were reported, Mordecai sent his pressing reply back.
Henry keeps before us that the messages to and fro by Hatach's hand were the only possible commerce between the shut-in queen and the mourner without.
Gill notes only that the messengers told Mordecai Esther's words.

themes: the bare relay as a hinge
a cause hanging in the silence

schools.summary: Keil gives the thrust: think not thou shalt escape in the king's house more than all the Jews.
Clarke reads the warning as confirming that Haman knew of the kinship, since Esther could no more escape in the palace than the rest.
Henry: it was her own cause, the decree excepting her not; wiser to risk a conditional death from the king than a certain death from the enemy.
Gill: Mordecai charged the messengers what answer to return.

Henry hears strong faith: deliverance will arise from another place though she fail, for God's covenant will not; silence would destroy her and her house; she was raised to the kingdom for such a time as this.

Wesley reads 'from another place' as strong faith believing against hope; Clarke is sure deliverance would come and Esther was the likely instrument (cf. the poor wise man who saved a city, Eccl. 9:14).

Ellicott renders 'enlargement' a breathing-space and takes 'from another place' with studied reserve for divine help, yet doubts Mordecai's earnestness of faith and finds the exchange devoid of any turning to God; 'thy father's house shall be destroyed' by the hand of God.
Gill states the case: if Esther holds her peace for fear of the danger.

debates.question: Does Mordecai's confidence in deliverance 'from another place' express a true and earnest faith in God?

sides.position: Yes — it is the language of strong faith, trusting God to save his people with her or without her
It refers to divine help but with studied reserve, betraying a lack of higher feeling and any turning to God

outliers.note: Reads 'thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed' as destruction by the hand of God, who having raised Esther will require the duty of her.

themes: for such a time as this

schools.summary: Keil reads the verse as the fruit of Mordecai's pressing monition — Esther sends back her reply, rising to meet the law.
Henry: she resolved to apply to the king, but not till she and her friends had first applied to God by fasting and prayer.
Gill: Esther bade the messengers return this answer to Mordecai.

Henry: Esther spoke as an Israelite with her eye up to God, joining fasting with prayer to a prayer-hearing God — a mistress praying with her maids — and as a queen, 'if I perish, I perish' (reasoning as the lepers, 2 Kings 7:4).

Clarke marvels again that God and prayer go unnamed, yet holds the humiliations must aim to turn away God's displeasure; Wesley reads the fast frankly as joined with fervent prayer, the maidens Jewesses or proselytes.
Keil reads the three days' fast as earnest humiliation seeking God's gracious help, though 'God' and 'prayer' are not named.
Gill: gather the Jews of Shushan to acquaint them; the Targum's twelve thousand priests is an exaggeration.

debates.question: Do the fast and mourning imply prayer to God, whom the book never names?

sides.position: Yes — the fast is a religious humiliation joined with prayer to a prayer-hearing God, seeking his gracious help
The silence of God and prayer is astonishing, though the humiliations must have been meant to turn away God's displeasure

schools.summary: Keil: Mordecai went from the open place before the court and did according to all Esther had commanded him.
Wesley reckons the three days and nights need not be counted full, since a part of a day is reputed a day in Scripture (cf. Matt. 12:40), and Esther went in on the third day.
Gill relays Jarchi's reading of the verb as 'transgressed,' Mordecai fasting through the passover (14th–16th Nisan) against the festival's joy.

outliers.note: Follows Jarchi in reading 'went his way' as 'transgressed' — Mordecai transgressing the passover by fasting through the feast of unleavened bread.
